sections.passage: A telephone conversation between a customer, Robert, and a holiday cottage booking agent, Helen. Robert is looking to rent a cottage for a family holiday in the Lake District. Helen asks about his requirements, and Robert explains that he needs accommodation for his family of four — himself, his wife, and two children aged 7 and 10. Helen describes several available properties. The first option is a two-bedroom cottage called Rose Cottage, located in the village of Ambleside. It costs 650 pounds per week during peak season and has a garden with views of Lake Windermere. The second option is a three-bedroom property called Oak Tree House in Grasmere, priced at 850 pounds per week. This one has a private garden, a fireplace, and is pet-friendly, which is important because Robert mentions they want to bring their dog. Robert asks about the facilities in Oak Tree House. Helen confirms it has a fully equipped kitchen, a washing machine, Wi-Fi, and a television with streaming services. The property also includes parking for two cars, which is convenient since Robert plans to drive. Robert asks about availability and Helen checks the system, confirming that Oak Tree House is available for the week of August 12th to 19th. Robert would like to book it and asks about the payment terms. Helen explains that a deposit of 200 pounds is required to secure the booking, with the balance due four weeks before arrival. There is also a refundable security deposit of 150 pounds. Robert asks about the cancellation policy, and Helen tells him that a full refund is available if cancellation is made more than six weeks before the arrival date. Between four and six weeks, a 50 percent refund is given, and less than four weeks before arrival, no refund is provided. Robert decides to book and provides his credit card details for the deposit.

title.en: Section 2 - Guided Tour of a Historic Factory
title.zh: 第二部分 - 参观历史工厂

sections.passage: Welcome to the Brookfield Pottery Visitor Centre. I'm Andrew Mitchell, and I'll be your guide today as we explore this remarkable site, which has been producing fine ceramics since 1832. The factory was founded by Josiah Brookfield, who came from a family of Staffordshire potters. At its peak in the late 19th century, the factory employed over 600 workers and exported its products to markets across Europe and North America. Today, while the factory operates on a smaller scale, it continues to produce high-quality handmade pottery using many of the same techniques that were used nearly two centuries ago. Our tour will begin in the museum, which is housed in the original Victorian building. Here you can see a collection of over 3,000 pieces of Brookfield pottery dating from the 1830s to the present day, including rare pieces from the Art Deco period of the 1920s and 1930s. The museum also has interactive displays showing how pottery is made, from preparing the clay to the final glazing process. After the museum, we'll move to the workshop, where you can watch the skilled craftspeople at work. The workshop offers demonstrations of throwing on a potter's wheel, hand painting, and kiln firing. If you'd like to try making your own pottery, we offer a hands-on workshop session on Wednesday and Saturday afternoons from 2 to 4 PM, which costs 25 pounds per person including materials. For children aged 6 to 12, we have a special junior pottery class every Sunday morning at 10 AM for 15 pounds. The tour finishes at the gift shop, where you can purchase handmade Brookfield pottery at factory prices. We also have a café serving homemade lunches and afternoon teas, using locally sourced ingredients wherever possible. The visitor centre is open Tuesday to Sunday, from 10 AM to 5 PM. Adult admission is 9 pounds, children under 16 are 5 pounds, and a family ticket for two adults and up to three children is 24 pounds. Please note that photography is allowed throughout the museum and workshop, but flash photography should be avoided near the display cases to protect the delicate glazes on the older pieces.

sections.passage: Two postgraduate students, Liam and Olivia, are discussing plans for their upcoming research field trip to study coastal erosion along the Norfolk coast. Their supervisor, Dr. Chen, has approved their proposal and they need to finalize the logistics. Liam has been researching potential study sites and has identified three locations that would be suitable: Happisburgh, which is experiencing some of the fastest rates of coastal erosion in Europe; Cromer, where new sea defenses have recently been installed; and Horsey, where there is a significant seal colony that could be affected by changing coastlines. Olivia has been working on the methodology. She proposes using a combination of GPS surveys, drone photography, and sediment sampling to document the current state of the coastline. They will compare their data with historical records from the Environment Agency, which has been monitoring erosion in the area since the 1990s. They plan to spend five days in the field, from Monday the 16th to Friday the 20th of September. On the first two days, they will survey Happisburgh, as it requires the most detailed investigation. Day three will be spent at Cromer, and the final two days at Horsey. Liam mentions that they will need to hire a drone for the aerial photography. He has found a company in Norwich that rents professional drones for 120 pounds per day, which includes insurance and a brief training session. Olivia suggests that they also need to arrange accommodation. She has found a holiday cottage in Sheringham for 80 pounds per night that can sleep four people, which would be suitable if their field assistant, Tom, joins them. Liam agrees and mentions that Dr. Chen may also visit for one or two days to provide guidance. They will need to bring their own laptops for data processing in the evenings, but Liam says he can borrow a GPS unit from the geography department. They agree to meet next Monday to finalize the equipment list and submit their risk assessment to Dr. Chen by the end of the week.

title.en: Section 4 - Lecture on Biodiversity in Urban Environments
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于城市环境中生物多样性的讲座

sections.passage: Good morning. Today's lecture is about urban biodiversity — a topic that might seem paradoxical, given that cities are often considered the antithesis of natural environments. Yet research over the past two decades has shown that urban areas can support surprisingly rich ecosystems, and that thoughtful urban design can significantly enhance biodiversity within city boundaries. Traditionally, conservation efforts have focused on protecting pristine wilderness areas. However, with over 55 percent of the world's population now living in cities — a figure projected to reach 68 percent by 2050 — urban environments are becoming increasingly important for biodiversity conservation. Cities can serve as refugia for certain species, particularly those that have adapted to human-modified landscapes. One of the most successful examples of urban biodiversity enhancement is the city of Singapore. Despite being one of the most densely populated countries in the world, Singapore has implemented its City in a Garden vision, which aims to integrate nature throughout the urban landscape. The project has created over 300 kilometres of park connectors linking green spaces across the city, green roofs on public buildings, and vertical gardens on the facades of high-rise structures. As a result, Singapore is home to over 400 species of birds, more than 350 species of butterflies, and numerous native plant species. In Europe, the city of Berlin has become a model for urban biodiversity. The city has over 2,500 public parks and green spaces, covering approximately 30 percent of its total area. Berlin's abandoned industrial sites, known as wastelands or brachen, have become unintentional wildlife havens, supporting rare species of plants, insects, and birds that have disappeared from the surrounding agricultural landscape. The city government has adopted a policy of protecting these areas rather than developing them. Green infrastructure is a key concept in urban biodiversity planning. This includes green roofs, which provide habitat for insects and birds while also reducing stormwater runoff and building temperatures. Rain gardens and bioswales filter pollutants from urban runoff before it enters waterways. Urban forests and tree-lined streets provide corridors that allow wildlife to move between larger green spaces. Research from Sheffield University found that gardens in British cities collectively cover more area than all the country's nature reserves combined, highlighting the potential of private gardens as biodiversity resources. Even small actions, such as planting native wildflowers, leaving areas of lawn unmown, and providing bird feeders and nest boxes, can make a significant difference to urban wildlife populations. However, urbanization also poses significant threats to biodiversity. Light pollution disrupts the behavior of nocturnal species, noise pollution affects bird communication and breeding success, and habitat fragmentation isolates populations, reducing genetic diversity. The heat island effect, where cities are significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas, can alter species composition and favor invasive species over native ones.

sections.passage:
Bread is one of the oldest prepared foods, with evidence of bread-making dating back at least 14,000 years — long before the advent of agriculture. Archaeological findings at the Shubayqa site in northeastern Jordan revealed charred remains of flatbread-like products made from wild cereals, predating the earliest known farming communities by several thousand years. This discovery challenged the long-held assumption that bread was a consequence of the agricultural revolution, suggesting instead that the desire for bread-like foods may have actually motivated early humans to begin cultivating grain.

The ancient Egyptians are widely credited with developing leavened bread around 3000 BC. Legend has it that the discovery was accidental — a batch of dough was left out and became contaminated with wild yeasts from the air, causing it to rise. When baked, this leavened dough produced a lighter, airier bread than the dense flatbreads that had been the norm. The Egyptians refined their bread-making techniques over centuries, developing a variety of shapes and recipes. Bread was so important to Egyptian society that it was used as a form of currency and was placed in tombs to sustain the dead in the afterlife.

The Greeks further advanced bread-making, introducing a wider range of grains and developing more sophisticated ovens. By the 5th century BC, Athens had become a major centre of bread production, with professional bakers selling a variety of breads in the city's agora, or marketplace. The Romans built upon Greek innovations and took bread-making to new heights. The Roman bread industry was highly organized, with regulated weights, quality standards, and a guild system for bakers. The remains of a bakery discovered in Pompeii reveal a remarkably modern operation, complete with mills, kneading machines, and large brick ovens. The Romans also developed the first mechanical flour mills, using water power to grind grain more efficiently.

During the Middle Ages in Europe, bread served a dual role as both food and tableware. Thick slices of stale bread, known as trenchers, were used as plates, absorbing the juices from meat and stew. The quality of bread consumed was a direct indicator of social status — the wealthy ate fine white bread made from sifted flour, while the poor subsisted on coarse, dark bread made from rye, barley, or mixed grains. By the 12th century, bakers in London were organized into a guild, and the Assize of Bread, first enacted in 1266, regulated the price and weight of bread for centuries.

The Industrial Revolution transformed bread production in the 19th century. The invention of steel roller mills in the 1870s made it possible to produce fine white flour cheaply and on a massive scale, making white bread accessible to all social classes for the first time. The development of commercial yeast eliminated the need for time-consuming sourdough starters, and the invention of mechanical bread-slicing machines in 1928 by Otto Frederick Rohwedder revolutionized the way bread was consumed. Pre-sliced bread became the standard, giving rise to the popular expression 'the best thing since sliced bread'. Today, bread remains a dietary staple for billions of people worldwide, though the types and methods of production vary enormously across cultures.

title.en: Passage 2 - The Impact of Light Pollution
title.zh: 文章2 - 光污染的影响

sections.passage:
For most of human history, the night sky was a source of wonder and inspiration. Today, however, two-thirds of the world's population can no longer see the Milky Way from their homes, and for residents of major cities, the night sky is often a featureless orange glow. This excessive and misdirected artificial light, known as light pollution, has grown at a rate of approximately 2 percent per year over the past few decades, and its consequences extend far beyond the loss of stargazing opportunities.

The ecological impact of light pollution is profound and wide-reaching. Artificial light at night disrupts the natural rhythms of virtually all living organisms. Many species of insects, birds, fish, and mammals rely on natural light cycles to regulate their behaviour, including migration, reproduction, feeding, and predator avoidance. Light pollution disrupts these cycles with potentially devastating consequences. Perhaps the most visible example is the effect on migratory birds. Millions of birds migrate at night, using the stars and the moon for navigation. Bright city lights disorient them, causing them to collide with illuminated buildings or circle light sources until they collapse from exhaustion. The Fatal Light Awareness Program estimates that up to one billion birds die each year in North America alone from collisions with illuminated structures.

Insects are also severely affected. Many species of moths, beetles, and other nocturnal insects are fatally attracted to artificial lights. A study in Germany found that the biomass of flying insects in protected areas declined by more than 75 percent over 27 years, with light pollution identified as one of the contributing factors alongside pesticide use and habitat loss. Since insects form the base of many food chains and play essential roles in pollination, their decline has cascading effects on entire ecosystems.

Human health is also compromised by excessive artificial light. Research has shown that exposure to artificial light at night suppresses the production of melatonin, a hormone that regulates sleep and has important antioxidant properties. Disrupted melatonin production has been linked to increased risks of sleep disorders, obesity, depression, and certain types of cancer, including breast and prostate cancer. A study published in the journal Environmental Health Perspectives found that residents of areas with the highest levels of outdoor nighttime light had a 17 percent higher risk of developing breast cancer compared to those in the darkest areas.

The economic cost of light pollution is also significant. In the United States alone, an estimated 30 percent of outdoor lighting is wasted — directed upwards or sideways where it serves no useful purpose. This wasted light costs approximately 3.3 billion dollars per year in energy costs and releases 21 million tons of carbon dioxide annually. However, the solutions to light pollution are relatively straightforward and cost-effective. Shielding lights to direct them downward, using warmer-colored LEDs instead of blue-white light, installing dimmers and timers, and simply turning off unnecessary lights can dramatically reduce light pollution while also saving energy and money.

title.en: Passage 3 - The Future of Space Exploration
title.zh: 文章3 - 太空探索的未来

sections.passage:
The 21st century has ushered in a new era of space exploration, fundamentally different from the government-led programmes of the Cold War era. The emergence of private space companies, advances in reusable rocket technology, and a renewed international interest in returning to the Moon and eventually reaching Mars have transformed the landscape of space exploration from a purely national endeavour into a dynamic, multi-stakeholder enterprise.

Perhaps the most significant development has been the rise of commercial space companies. SpaceX, founded by Elon Musk in 2002, has dramatically reduced the cost of reaching orbit by developing reusable rocket boosters. Its Falcon 9 rocket can land itself on a drone ship after delivering its payload to orbit, and the same booster can be reflown multiple times, reducing launch costs by an estimated 30 percent. The company's Starship vehicle, currently in development, promises to be the most powerful rocket ever built and is central to Musk's stated goal of establishing a human settlement on Mars. Jeff Bezos's Blue Origin and Richard Branson's Virgin Galactic are pursuing different approaches to commercial spaceflight, with Blue Origin focusing on lunar landers and orbital habitats, and Virgin Galactic offering suborbital space tourism flights.

NASA's Artemis programme represents the United States' commitment to returning astronauts to the Moon. The programme aims to land the first woman and the next man on the lunar surface and establish a sustainable human presence there. The Artemis Base Camp, planned for the lunar south pole, would serve as a testing ground for technologies needed for eventual Mars missions, including life support systems, resource extraction from lunar regolith, and long-duration habitation. The European Space Agency, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, and the Canadian Space Agency are all partners in the Artemis programme, contributing various components and capabilities.

China has emerged as a major space power with ambitious plans of its own. The China National Space Administration has successfully landed rovers on both the Moon and Mars, and is constructing its own modular space station, Tiangong, which became fully operational in 2022. China has announced plans to send astronauts to the Moon by 2030 and to establish a joint lunar research base with Russia at the Moon's south pole.

The scientific rationale for space exploration extends far beyond national prestige. Space-based research has yielded practical benefits for life on Earth, including advances in telecommunications, weather forecasting, GPS navigation, and Earth observation for climate monitoring. The International Space Station has served as a unique laboratory for research in materials science, biology, and medicine that cannot be replicated on Earth due to the effects of gravity. Astronaut Scott Kelly's year-long stay on the ISS, during which his health was compared to that of his twin brother Mark who remained on Earth, provided invaluable data on the effects of long-duration spaceflight on the human body.

However, space exploration also raises important ethical and practical questions. The growing problem of space debris — thousands of defunct satellites and millions of fragments of debris orbiting the Earth at high velocities — poses a serious threat to both crewed and uncrewed missions. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, which governs activities in space, was drafted when space exploration was the domain of only two superpowers and may need updating to address the complexities of a more crowded and commercially driven space environment. Questions of resource rights, planetary protection, and the equitable sharing of the benefits of space exploration will need to be resolved as humanity extends its reach further into the solar system.

prompt.en: The table below shows the number of tourists visiting five different countries in 2000, 2010, and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
prompt.zh: 下面的表格显示了2000年、2010年和2020年五个不同国家的游客数量。通过选择和报告主要特征来总结信息，并在相关地方进行比较。至少写150个单词。

prompt.en: Some people argue that the government should spend more money on public services rather than wasting it on the arts. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
prompt.zh: 一些人认为政府应该在公共服务上花更多的钱，而不是浪费在艺术上。你在多大程度上同意或不同意？给出你回答的理由，并包括你自己的知识或经验中任何相关的例子。至少写250个单词。
